summary:
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the federal statutes governing gender identity and sexual orientation apply within the okrug unaltered. No regional deviation from the national position has been identified, so the national assessment governs what a visitor faces here.

Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are banned outright. The law signed by President Putin in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year. Gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, so a visitor's papers cannot be brought into line with their presentation: any police, hotel or transport identity check reads a mismatch that no supporting document can resolve.

The expanded "propaganda" law criminalises public expression that promotes non-traditional relationships and, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Administrative penalties reach 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, and repeat offences escalate to criminal prosecution with up to four years' imprisonment. Foreign nationals who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings tell LGBT travellers precisely that.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation in the designated movement carries 2-6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6-10 years under Article 282.2. Same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, while same-sex sexual activity is not itself criminalised.

Entry risk is severe: the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols, roughly 98 of them administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty across 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, so residents have no domestic route to correcting their legal status. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, removing in-country access to gender-affirming care.

The UK Home Office records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or by its repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection.

Residents who are subjected to the propaganda statutes or the extremism regime face the same administrative fines, detention and Article 282.2 sentences that apply to visitors, and the 2023 designation has produced convictions against people for displaying symbols as well as for alleged participation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no material specific to Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. No prosecution, raid or administrative case under the propaganda or extremism statutes within the okrug is documented here, and the absence of such records should not be read as evidence that enforcement is absent in the okrug.

All enforcement figures cited, including the 101 convictions, the eighteenfold rise in cases and the fine revenue, are national totals. Their distribution across the okrug is not sourced, and no okrug-level breakdown was located.

The conversion-therapy case documented by BBC Russian took place in a different federal subject and is reported as evidence of the coercive pattern faced by trans people nationally, not as a finding about this okrug.

Whether okrug-level police, migration or medical authorities apply any additional screening to trans visitors, beyond the national framework, is unresolved: no source in the inventory addresses it.

The dating of the UK Home Office note is inconsistent across the inventory, giving a June 2025 publication with a later page update; the currency of its figures beyond that point is unresolved.
